description: Hi! I'm joining the NASA Space Apps Challenge to build health monitoring software for astronauts. I love coding and problem-solving, and I'm looking for teammates skilled in UI/UX design, data analysis, or development to build an impactful space tech solution together!
summary: Crew Health Monitor is a self-monitoring tool for astronauts on long-duration missions, where radiation, isolation, altered gravity and a closed environment can cause immune changes, bone loss, cardiovascular problems and behavioral health issues. Crews often have to spot these changes in themselves. The app collects a daily check-in covering vital signs, sleep, exercise, radiation dose, mood, symptoms and a quick reaction-time test. It compares each reading with the astronaut’s own baseline and with safety thresholds, rates five body systems, and gives prioritized actions, including when to contact the flight surgeon. It works offline, stores data locally, and exports for medical review. Catching small trends early helps keep crews safe on missions such as Moon and Mars, where real-time support is limited.
details:
Crew Health Monitor is a web app that lets an astronaut on a long-duration mission track their own health and decide what to do about it, without waiting for ground support.

How it works: The astronaut logs a daily check-in: resting heart rate, blood pressure, SpO₂, temperature, body mass, sleep, exercise minutes, dosimeter radiation dose, mood, stress, and symptoms. A built-in 5-tap reaction test measures cognitive and fatigue changes. The app builds a personal baseline from the first 5 days, then compares each new reading against it and against mission safety thresholds. It rates five body systems green, amber or red: heart and circulation, immune system, bones and muscle, sleep and mind, and radiation exposure. It then gives a ranked list of next steps and tells the astronaut when to contact the flight surgeon.

Benefits and impact: It addresses the hazards named in the challenge: radiation, isolation, altered gravity and closed environments. Because it works from each person’s own baseline, it can catch slow drifts such as bone and muscle loss, rising resting heart rate, worsening sleep or low mood. It runs offline in a browser, which matters when communication is delayed, and it exports to CSV for the medical team.

Tools: HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript in a single file, SVG charts, and browser local storage. It needs no special hardware.

Creativity and design factors: Status is shown as one clear verdict plus actions, so a tired crew member can act quickly. We considered offline use, privacy (data stays on the device), and personal baselines rather than population averages. Thresholds are illustrative and the tool is decision support, not diagnosis.
